title: Portage College Tells Indian Students to Seek Legal Advice After Mass Work Permit Rejections
excerpt: The Alberta college says it cannot overturn IRCC decisions and has advised affected graduates to retain key documents as thousands face an uncertain future following post-graduation work permit refusals.
body:
College Draws a Clear Line

Portage College in Calgary has told protesting Indian students that while it sympathises with their plight, it cannot reverse the immigration decisions that have upended their lives.

https://x.com/Sammy_canada2/status/2079518039431589907

In an update posted to its website on July 21, the college said it "continues to seek clarification regarding this issue" but made its limitations explicit: "IRCC has sole authority over immigration decisions. Portage College cannot approve, reverse, vary, or require reconsideration of an IRCC decision," according to a FAQ published alongside the update, as reported by the Times of India.

The college has scheduled a follow-up meeting with representatives of the affected student group for next week. "This meeting will provide an opportunity to continue our dialogue, answer questions where we are able, and share any new information that becomes available," the college stated.

What Happened to the Students

Thousands of Indian students enrolled in Portage College's business management diploma programme. After completing their studies, they applied for post-graduation work permits — the standard pathway that allows international graduates to remain and work in Canada for up to three years, building eligibility for permanent residency.

But Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada rejected the applications, determining that the programmes were not eligible for PGWPs. The refusals have left graduates in legal limbo, facing the prospect of having to leave Canada despite having invested years and substantial tuition fees in their education.

The students have contested the rejections on two fronts. They point out that graduates from the same college and the same programmes received PGWP approvals before July 7, suggesting an abrupt policy shift. They also allege that IRCC quietly changed its rules to make non-credit programmes ineligible for the permit.

IRCC, for its part, has maintained that no rule change was made.

Retain Everything, the College Warns

In practical guidance that underscores the severity of the situation, Portage College has advised affected students to keep copies of all documents that may be relevant to future applications, reconsideration requests, or legal proceedings. The list includes study permits, letters of acceptance, enrolment records, programme completion documents, transcripts, PGWP applications, IRCC refusal letters, officer notes, and all correspondence with IRCC or immigration representatives.

The college has also emphasised that its own institutional letters do not establish PGWP eligibility or guarantee approval of any immigration application — a caveat that highlights the gap between what students may have been led to expect and the reality of Canada's immigration system.

"Any student who wishes to pursue a legal or immigration process must do so independently or through an authorized representative."

— Portage College, published FAQ

A Pattern Across Canadian Colleges

The Portage College situation is part of a broader crisis facing Indian students in Canada. In recent years, thousands of international students — the majority from India — have found themselves caught between institutional promises and immigration realities. Fraudulent letters of acceptance, shifting eligibility criteria, and stricter enforcement by IRCC have created a volatile landscape for students who often take on significant debt to study abroad.

Canada rejected the majority of Indian study permit applications in 2025, with authorities uncovering more than 14,000 potentially fraudulent letters of acceptance, according to Reuters. The tightened scrutiny has extended to post-graduation work permits, where new language proficiency and field-of-study documentation requirements have tripped up students who were unaware of the changes.

What's Next for Affected Students

Students whose PGWPs have been refused face time-sensitive deadlines. Under Canadian immigration rules, they may have a limited window to apply for restoration of status or file reconsideration requests. The college has directed affected graduates to the government of Canada's official PGWP information and urged them to seek independent legal counsel promptly.

For those dealing with the emotional toll, Portage College has pointed to 211 Alberta, a mental health and community services helpline — an acknowledgement that the crisis extends well beyond immigration paperwork for the young Indians caught in its crosshairs.
